html:
I’ve done research on moving sound sources. Let me briefly explain the principle first, then play you some simulated audio, using “Listen to Mom” by Jay Chou, the Taiwanese pop superstar, as the example.

By “weaker,” the question means a drop in frequency plus a drop in amplitude. Also, ideally the speed of sound in a given medium doesn’t change, so the drop in “speed” in the question’s description must really mean a drop in frequency.

The asker presumably means that we run away from the sound, in the direction it is traveling. So let’s look at it from a different angle: we stay put, and the source moves away from us. Note that although the two scenarios have similar effects, they aren’t equivalent.

In the first case, the frequency the ear hears is f=c−vrcf0

and in the second, f=cc+vsf0

Here f is the frequency received at the ear, f0 the frequency of the source, c the speed of sound, vr the speed of the receiver and vs the speed of the source, with both assumed to move at constant speed. This is the famous Doppler effect, which other answers have mentioned too.

Why not go with what the asker meant, instead of swapping in the other scenario? Because I study moving sources, not moving people, and I didn’t want to change my code…

Let’s make it more intuitive.

Suppose the source is at [0,0] and you’re standing at [−5,0]. If neither you nor the source moves, the number of wavefronts reaching you each second stays the same: the wavelength is constant, and so is the frequency.

Now let the source move in the positive x direction. You can see the waves on the left spread out, so fewer wavefronts reach you each second: the wavelength grows and the frequency drops.

Let’s make it even more intuitive. Please welcome Jay Chou to the stage!

Friendly reminder: to protect your hearing, turn your headphone volume down before you listen.


First we put Jay in an ambulance and have him race past you at 120 km/h (ignoring wind), singing “Listen to Mom.”


Now Jay moves away from you at 30 km/h. He starts 1.5 m from you and moves at right angles to the line between you.

Watch this video in the original Zhihu answer

00:06


The frequency shift isn’t very obvious, is it? Now let’s take it up to 100 km/h and get ready for the highway.

Watch this video in the original Zhihu answer

00:06

Jay’s voice is getting deeper and deeper, and quieter and quieter. Deeper because of the frequency shift; quieter because of geometric spreading: if r is the distance between you, the sound pressure you receive falls off as 1/r. That decay gets in the way of going faster. Any faster, and before long you wouldn’t be able to hear what he’s singing at all. To bring out the frequency shift, we’ve decided to defy physics and throw away the 1/r! Here’s a comparison at 300 km/h, with and without 1/r.


Again without 1/r, let’s see what happens when the source flees at the speed of sound.

Watch this video in the original Zhihu answer

00:06 The source fleeing at the speed of sound

The result: Jay sounds more and more down.


What about twice the speed of sound? (Again ignoring 1/r.)

The lyrics are even harder to make out.

Getting bored of the standard stuff? Let’s spice things up.

Let’s hear what a guinea pig’s high-pitched squeal sounds like with Doppler added. Watch the video below, and listen for the guinea pig’s squeal from the 5-second mark.

OK, we extract the audio from the 5-second mark on. Now the guinea pig makes the same squeal, except that it’s sprinting away from you at five times the speed of sound. What do you hear?

Yep: the guinea pig has evolved into its final form.
